[QUESTION] How did the median house price change in community districts with upzoned lots compared to those with downzoned lots between 1998 and 2003?
<<<EVIDENCE>>>

The median house price change in community districts that experienced rezoning between 1998 and 2003 varied depending on the type of rezoning. As shown in Table F, community districts with upzoned lots saw a median house price increase of 62.5%. In contrast, districts with downzoned lots experienced a smaller increase of 54.9%.

![Median House Price Change](image6)

This comparison indicates that upzoning, which often allows for higher density and potentially more development, was associated with a higher increase in median house prices compared to downzoning, which typically restricts development density. The data suggests that upzoning might have spurred greater demand or investment in these areas, reflected in the higher appreciation of house prices.

passages.text: [9] The fact that down zoning s were in areas  with lower building activity than the City  median indicates that down zoning s were  not necessarily a response to particularly  high rates of new building. Perhaps the  most interesting finding is that the areas  that saw the greatest demand were the  areas that were contextual-only rezoned.  As discussed above, the precise impact of a  contextual rezoning can vary a great deal.  It may not limit development, but it may  limit developers’ flexibility to provide build- ing designs that the market prefers or that  would be more affordable.

[4] We estimate that in 2003, the Zoning Reso- lution allowed for approximately 6 billion  square feet of residential development  capacity citywide; Brooklyn had the high- est capacity, followed by Manhattan, then  Queens. Between 2003 and 2007, the City  rezoned almost   $18\%$   of the City’s total  lot area. Of the 188,000 lots that were  included in a City-initiated rezoning action,  almost   $63\%$   were subject to a contextual- only rezoning,   $23\%$   were downzoned and   $14\%$   were upzoned.

[6] Finally, we look at demand by examining the  rate of new construction in the community  districts where rezoned lots were located.  Specifically, we look at the number of certifi- cates of occupancy—the final permit issued  by the City before a residential building can  be occupied—issued between 1998 and  2003.  As Table G reveals, upzoned lots were  located in areas that had about the same level  of development as the City during that time  (as measured by the number of certificates  of occupancy issued). Downzoned lots were  in areas that saw significantly less building  activity, while contextual-only rezoned lots  were in areas that had much higher rates of  development than the City median. These  findings have several important implica- tions. The fact the upzonings took place in  areas with average levels of development  may signal that the upzonings will have to  lead, rather than follow, the market. It may  be appropriate for upzonings to try to chan- nel growth into areas where the market has  not yet signaled interest if, for example, the  City believes infrastructure in those areas is  underused, or if the City plans to upgrade  infrastructure it believes was holding devel- opment back. On the other hand, it could  be that the average development patterns in  the areas with upzoned lots signals that the  market isn’t interested in the area for reasons  that City initiatives won’t cure.

[3] Finally, we looked at the home ownership  rate of rezoned areas, and found a pattern  similar to that of household income. As  Table C shows, upzoned lots were located  in areas with a much lower homeowner- ship rate than the City median   $(30.8\%$    compared to   $44.8\%$  ). Downzoned lots also  were in areas with home ownership rates  that were lower than the City median, but  slightly higher than the rate for upzoned  areas. Again, the biggest difference was for  the contextual-only rezoned lots, which  were located in areas with very high rates of  home ownership   $(65\%)$  .

[1] Our analysis classifies as “contextual-only”  any zoning change to a lot that does not  increase or decrease its residential devel- opment capacity by more than  $10\%$  . Most  of the lots rezoned between 2003 and  2007 fall into this category (particularly in  Staten Island and Queens).

[2] n   Upzoned.  We define a lot as upzoned,  if the rezoning increased its resi- dential development capacity to at  least  $10\%$   more than its pre-rezoning  capacity. n   Downzoned.  We define a lot as down- zoned if the rezoning decreased its  residential development capacity to  less than  $90\%$   of its pre-rezoning  capacity. n   Contextual-only rezoned.  We define  a lot as “contextual-only rezoned” if  the rezoning changed some aspects of  what can be built on the lot, but did  not significantly change its residential  development capacity (specifically, by  more than  $10\%$  ). A more complete  discussion of contextual-only rezon- ings can be found on page 5.

Beyond the present binary classiﬁcation task, one could ex- plore a sequential formulation predicting whether the next turn is likely to be an attack as a discus- sion unfolds, capturing conversational dynamics such as sustained escalation.

[5] Crowdsourced ﬁltering.  Starting from these can- didate sets, we use crowdsourcing to vet each con- versation and select a subset that are perceived by humans to either stay civil throughout (“on- track” conversations), or start civil but end with a  personal attack  (“awry-turning” conversations). To inform the design of this human-ﬁltering pro- cess and to check its effectiveness, we start from a seed set of 232 conversations manually ver- iﬁed by the authors to end in personal attacks (more details about the selection of the seed set and its role in the crowd-sourcing process can be found in Appendix  A ). We take particular care to not over-constrain crowdworker interpretations of what personal attacks may be, and to separate tox- icity from civil disagreement, which is recognized as a key aspect of effective collaborations ( Coser , 1956 ;  De Dreu and Weingart ,  2003 ).

[9] Trained toxicity:  We also compare with the tox- icity score of the exchange from the Perspective API classiﬁer—a perhaps unfair reference point, since this supervised system was trained on addi- tional human-labeled training examples from the same domain and since it was used to create the very data on which we evaluate. This results in an accuracy of   $60.5\%$  ; combining trained toxicity with our pragmatic features achieves   $64.9\%$  .

[7] We consider the following balanced prediction task: given a pair of conversations, which one will eventually lead to a personal attack? We ex- tract all features from the very ﬁrst exchange in a conversation—i.e., a comment-reply pair, like those illustrated in our introductory example (Fig- ure  1 ). We use logistic regression and report ac- curacies on a leave-one-page-out cross validation, such that in each fold, all conversation pairs from a given talk page are held out as test data and pairs from all other pages are used as training data (thus preventing the use of page-speciﬁc information). [QUESTION] What evaluation aspects and metrics are associated with the CRUD evaluation framework?
<<<EVIDENCE>>>

The CRUD evaluation framework is designed to assess both retrieval and generation quality. It focuses on the following evaluation aspects:

- **Creative Generation**: The ability to generate content creatively.
- **Knowledge-intensive QA**: Handling questions that require significant background knowledge.
- **Error Correction**: The ability to detect and correct errors in generation or retrieval processes.
- **Summarization**: The capacity to effectively summarize information.

For these aspects, CRUD employs several quantitative metrics to measure performance:

- **BLEU**: A metric for evaluating the quality of text which has been machine-translated from one language to another.
- **ROUGE-L**: A set of metrics for evaluating automatic summarization and machine translation, particularly focusing on the longest common subsequence.
- **BertScore**: This metric leverages BERT's contextual embeddings to evaluate the similarity between candidate and reference sentences, focusing on semantic similarity.
- **RAGQuestEval**: A specific evaluation metric tailored for assessing RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) systems[12].

[QUESTION] How does the performance of different models and decoding methods compare in terms of generating commonsense inferences, and what impact does the amount of training data have on these performances?
<<<EVIDENCE>>>

The performance of different models and decoding methods in generating commonsense inferences can be compared across several metrics and conditions, with the COMET framework showing the most promising results. Here is a detailed comparison based on the provided multi-modal evidence:

### Comparison of Decoding Methods

The table on decoding methods (Figure 1) highlights various strategies used within the COMET framework:

- **Greedy decoding** performs best among the automated methods with an average score of 77.53, while the human baseline is 86.18.
- Other methods like beam search and random sampling show lower performance, with beam search (2 beams) achieving an average score of 63.29. 

![Decoding Method Comparison](image5)

### Impact of Training Data Amount

Figure 2 provides insight into how varying the amount of training data affects performance metrics such as Perplexity (PPL), BLEU-2, N/T, and N/U:

- Training with 1% of the data results in higher perplexity (23.81) and lower BLEU-2 score (5.08).
- Increasing the data to 10% significantly improves these metrics (PPL: 13.74, BLEU-2: 12.72), and further improvements are seen with 50% and full training datasets.
- The FULL training dataset yields the best results with the lowest PPL (11.13) and highest BLEU-2 (14.34).

![Training Data Impact](image8)

### Model Performance Comparison

Figure 4 compares different models including COMET and its variants, LSTM, and CKBG:

- **COMET (with and without pretraining)** outperforms other models with a perplexity of 4.32, a score of 95.25, and near-human performance (91.69).
- COMET - RELTOK also shows strong performance, particularly in converting relation tokens.
- The LSTM and CKBG models have significantly lower scores and higher perplexity, indicating less effective commonsense inference generation.

![Model Comparison](image2)

### Conclusion

- **COMET** consistently achieves the highest performance across different evaluation metrics and configurations, especially when fully trained with pretraining and greedy decoding methods[1][12].
- Performance metrics improve significantly with increased training data, underscoring the importance of extensive data for training effective commonsense inference models.
- Greedy decoding stands out among automated methods, but human validation remains the gold standard for the highest quality commonsense inferences.

These comparisons and insights illustrate the effectiveness of COMET and the impact of both decoding methods and training data volume on generating high-quality commonsense inferences.

2. **Management Oversight**: The Board oversees management activities to ensure they align with the company’s strategic objectives. This includes supervising the execution of operations by the operating officers and ensuring accountability across all levels of management.

3. **Interaction with Other Governance Bodies**: The Board receives suggestions from the Executive Appointment Meeting and the Executive Compensation Meeting, which helps in shaping decisions about leadership appointments and compensation structures.

4. **Audit and Supervision**: The Board works alongside the Audit & Supervisory Board to ensure rigorous audit processes are in place, maintaining transparency and accountability in financial and operational reporting.

5. **Sustainability and Reporting**: Involvement in sustainability meetings ensures that the Board incorporates environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations into the corporate strategy.

The structure also includes a referral and report system where operating officers are required to report to the Board, allowing for comprehensive oversight and informed decision-making.

The process to determine whether there is a significant economic incentive includes a comparison of a vehicle’s estimated market value at the time the option is exercisable with the guaranteed resale value to determine the customer’s economic incentive to exercise. Sales return reserves for automotive sales with resale value guarantees are estimated based on historical experience plus consideration for expected future market values. On a quarterly basis, we assess the estimated market values of vehicles under our buyback options program to determine whether there have been changes to the likelihood of future product returns. As we accumulate more data related to the buyback values of our vehicles or as market conditions change, there may be material changes to their estimated values. Due to price adjustments we made to our vehicle offerings during 2020, we estimated that there is a greater likelihood that customers will exercise their buyback options that were provided prior to such adjustments. As a result, along with the estimated variable consideration related to normal future product returns for vehicles sold under the buyback options program, we adjusted our sales return reserve on vehicles previously sold under our buyback options program resulting in a reduction of automotive sales revenues of   $\S72$  million for the year ended December 31, 2020. The inclusion of inconsistency loss in text summarization models has a significant impact on their performance, as evidenced by improvements in both objective metrics like ROUGE scores[12] and subjective human evaluations[8].

### ROUGE Scores
The comparison of methods with and without inconsistency loss using ROUGE metrics shows clear differences:
- **End-to-end model with inconsistency loss** achieves higher ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L scores compared to its counterpart without inconsistency loss. For instance:

  - ROUGE-L: **37.13**

![Broader methods comparison](image7)

In terms of human evaluations, summarization models are assessed on three criteria: informativity, conciseness, and readability:
- The model with inconsistency loss scored highest on informativity (**3.58**) and readability (**3.70**), indicating that it generates more informative and readable summaries than those without inconsistency loss[8].

The effect of employing inconsistency loss is quantified by the average inconsistency rate:
- The inconsistency rate significantly drops from **0.198** to **0.042** when inconsistency loss is included[9].

### Key Climate-Related Risk Types Considered by the Bank

The bank identifies and assesses various climate-related risk types in alignment with regulatory compliance, market dynamics, and environmental sustainability principles. These risk types and their assessments are outlined below:

#### **1. Current Regulation**
The bank complies with existing environmental laws and integrates risk assessment processes through frameworks such as the Social and Environmental Management System (SEMS)[6][1]. This ensures that large loans are screened for environmental and social risks, preventing violations of laws.

#### **2. Emerging Regulation**
Transition risks arise from regulatory changes aimed at shifting to a low-carbon economy. The bank evaluates potential impacts on its credit portfolio, especially for sectors like coal, thermal, and infrastructure. Scenario analyses are employed to understand these risks better.

#### **3. Technology**
Digital banking and information security practices are assessed for their impact on climate change risks. The bank leverages low-carbon digital products, which are not considered significant contributors to climate risks.

#### **4. Legal**
The bank ensures compliance with environmental laws in its loan projects to minimize litigation risks. It also confirms that no direct liabilities arise from climate-related legal claims.

#### **5. Market**
Climate change impacts market dynamics, influencing demand for financial products such as green loans or low-carbon digital products. The bank manages these risks through well-defined policies like Market Risk and Investment Policies.

#### **6. Reputation**
Reputation risks due to community and customer perceptions are mitigated by integrating Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) strategies[10], publishing GHG emissions data, and engaging stakeholders through sustainability initiatives.

#### **7. Acute Physical**
Acute physical risks, such as natural disasters, pose threats to credit portfolios and infrastructure. The bank conducts scenario analysis and employs Business Continuity and Disaster Response systems to address these challenges.

#### **8. Chronic Physical**
Long-term climate effects are managed by leveraging granular data and tools for assessing risks like health and crop pattern disruptions[8].

![Key Climate-Related Risk Types](image2)

### Comprehensive Assessment Approach
- The bank utilizes frameworks like SEMS for environmental and social risk evaluation.
- Scenario analysis tools help gauge the impact of acute and chronic physical risks and regulatory transitions.
- ESG strategies and sustainability reporting are integrated into operations, ensuring alignment with broader environmental goals.

By addressing these risks holistically, the bank demonstrates its commitment to mitigating climate-related challenges while maintaining regulatory and operational resilience.

We use two crowdsourcing tasks. First, we provide workers with a scenario and ask them to write in- structions. The workers are encouraged to explore the environment and interact with it. We then seg- ment the instructions to sentences automatically. In the second task, workers are presented with the segmented sentences in order and asked to execute them. After ﬁnishing a sentence, the workers re- quest the next sentence. The workers do not see the original scenario. Figure  4  shows a scenario and the written segmented paragraph. Here's a breakdown of the diagram:

1. **Instruction Processing:**
   - The instruction "Turn left and go to the red oil drum" is represented as text, denoted by $\bar{x}$.
   - This text is processed by a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to map it to a representation $\bar{\bf x}$.

2. **Initial Observation:**
   - An initial panorama image ${\bf I}_{P}$ is input into a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to generate an image feature map ${\bf F}_{0}$.

3. **LingUNet Generation:**
   - LingUNet uses the text representation $\bar{\bf x}$ to generate text kernels $\mathbf{K}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{K}_{4}^{-}$.
   - A sequence of convolutions maps the initial image feature ${\bf F}_{0}$ to layered feature maps: $\mathbf{F}_{1}, \dots, \mathbf{F}_{4}$.
   - These are combined with the text-conditioned kernels to produce text-conditioned feature maps $\mathbf{G}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{G}_{4}$.

4. **Deconvolution:**
   - The text-conditioned feature maps are deconvolved to produce $\mathbf{H}_{1}, \ldots, \mathbf{H}_{4}$.
   - The first layer, $\mathbf{H}_{1}$, is used to calculate a goal probability distribution, $P_{g}$.

5. **Goal Location and Action Determination:**

   - Given the current pose at step $t$, denoted as $p_{t}$, a goal mask $\mathbf{M}_{t}$ is computed.
   - This goal mask is input into an RNN to produce actions (e.g., TURNLEFT, FORWARD).

Overall, the architecture integrates visual and textual inputs to guide navigation, where the system follows the instruction to turn left and reach the designated target based on its learned mappings and probability distributions.

[1] We introduce two new benchmark tasks with different levels of complexity of goal prediction and action generation. L ANI  is a 3D navigation environment and corpus, where an agent navigates between landmarks. The corpus includes 6,000 sequences of natural language instructions, each containing on average 4.7 instructions. C HAI  is a corpus of 1,596 instruction sequences, each in- cluding 7.7 instructions on average, for C HALET , a 3D house environment ( Yan et al. ,  2018 ). In- structions combine navigation and simple manipu- lation, including moving objects and opening con- tainers. Both tasks require solving language chal- lenges, including spatial and temporal reasoning, as well as complex perception and planning prob- lems. While L ANI  provides a task where most in- structions include a single goal, the C HAI  instruc- tions often require multiple intermediate goals. For example, the household instruction in Fig- ure  1  can be decomposed to eight goals: opening the cupboard, picking each item and moving it to the cupboard, and closing the cupboard. Achiev- ing each goal requires multiple actions of differ- ent types, including moving and acting on objects. This allows us to experiment with a simple varia- tion of our model to generate intermediate goals.

[2] We compare our approach to multiple recent methods. Experiments on the L ANI  navigation task indicate that decomposing goal prediction and action generation signiﬁcantly improves in- struction execution performance. \[ \text{ROCE} = \frac{\text{Operating Income}}{\text{Capital Employed}} \]

**Operating Income** for 2023 is provided as $1,795 million.

- **Current Liabilities**: $8,979 million

\[ \text{Capital Employed} = 15,803 - 8,979 = 6,824 \text{ million} \]

Plugging these values into the ROCE formula:

\[ \text{ROCE} = \frac{1,795}{6,824} \approx 0.263 \]

Therefore, the Return on Capital Employed for the fiscal year ending January 28, 2023, is approximately 0.263, when rounded to three decimal places.

<<<EVIDENCE>>>

The financial performance between fiscal years 2019 and 2020 was influenced by several key factors, as illustrated by the changes in operating expenses and other financial metrics.

First, the increase in operating expenses was a significant factor. From the data on page 1, we observe that operating expenses rose from $9,296 million in 2019 to $12,566 million in 2020, an increase of $3,270 million. This increase was primarily driven by higher research and development costs, marketing and sales expenses, and general and administrative expenses. These increases are detailed in the textual descriptions on page 2, where it is explained that the rise in these expenses was largely due to increased headcount and related costs[2][12][6].

![Operating Expenses](image2)

Moreover, the gains on strategic investments, as shown in Figure 1, decreased from $542 million in 2019 to $427 million in 2020, a decline of $115 million. This decrease negatively impacted overall financial performance by reducing the company's non-operating income[2].

![Gains on Strategic Investments, Net](image2)

On the other hand, there was a decrease in 'Other expense' from $94 million in 2019 to $18 million in 2020, a reduction of $76 million, which provided some relief to the financial performance.

Additionally, Figure 2 reveals a significant negative variance in the 'Benefit from (Provision for) Income Taxes,' which shifted from a positive $127 million in 2019 to a negative $(580) million in 2020, a variance of $(707) million. This change also contributed to the overall financial performance challenges[2][1].

![Benefit from (Provision for) Income Taxes](image1)

In summary, the overall financial performance was negatively impacted by increased operating expenses and a decline in gains on strategic investments, while a decrease in other expenses provided some mitigation. The substantial negative change in income tax benefit further exacerbated the financial challenges faced in fiscal year 2020 compared to 2019.

[QUESTION] What is the maximum term for options under ESOP schemes XIX to XXVIII and XXIX to XXXV?
<<<EVIDENCE>>>

The maximum term for options under different ESOP schemes is defined by the lapse period from the date of vesting.

For options granted under **ESOP Scheme XIX to XXVIII**, they will lapse if not exercised by the employee within **4 years** from the respective dates of vesting. This means that employees have up to four years to exercise their options from when they vest[2].

For options under **ESOP Scheme XXIX to XXXV**, the lapse period is shorter. These options will lapse if not exercised within **2 years** from the respective dates of vesting. This shorter term requires employees to act more quickly to take advantage of their stock options[11].

![ESOP Terms](image7)

These terms are crucial for employees to understand as they dictate the time frame within which they must exercise their stock options to benefit from them. Failure to exercise within these time frames results in the options lapsing, meaning they become void and cannot be exercised thereafter.

The contextual augmentation method illustrated in Figure 1 demonstrates the use of a bi-directional RNN language model to enhance data augmentation by generating new sentences. In this process, a given sentence such as "the actors are fantastic" is taken as input. The model highlights a key word, in this case, "actors," and replaces it with contextually appropriate synonyms or related words like "performances," "films," "movies," and "stories." This substitution is guided by the model's understanding of the sentence context, ensuring that the overall sentiment, which is positive in this case, is preserved.[6][2]

The primary goal of this method is to expand the dataset with diverse yet semantically consistent sentences. By doing so, it enriches the training data, potentially improving the model's robustness and generalization capabilities. The visual representation in Figure 1 effectively captures this process by showing the flow from the original sentence to the augmented versions, along with maintaining the associated sentiment label.

[QUESTION] How do Denoising Autoencoder (DAE) and Variational Autoencoder (VAE) compare in terms of their performance on style transfer accuracy and content similarity across different latent spaces and datasets?
<<<EVIDENCE>>>

DAE and VAE exhibit comparable performance in style transfer accuracy and content similarity across different latent spaces and datasets. However, there are nuances in their performance that are highlighted through various analyses and visualizations presented in the figures and tables. Here are the key findings: 

**Performance in Latent Spaces:** 

From the **classification accuracy table (Figure 1)**, it is evident that both DAE and VAE perform similarly in style space and complete space, with perfect or near-perfect accuracy (0.97) on the Yelp dataset and high accuracy (0.82 for DAE and 0.81 for VAE) on the Amazon dataset. The content space shows slightly lower performance but still demonstrates that both models are capable of utilizing this space effectively.

![Classification Accuracy](image2)

**Visual Separation in Latent Spaces:** 

The **t-SNE plots (Figure 2)** provide a visual representation of how DAE and VAE separate style and content spaces. In the style space, DAE achieves more distinct clustering of positive and negative samples, indicating better separation. For content space, both models show overlapping clusters, suggesting less separation but still meaningful representation.

![t-SNE Plots](image8)

**Overall Performance Metrics:** 

The **performance comparison table (Figure 3)** further supports these findings. For the Yelp dataset, DAE achieves a higher style transfer accuracy (STA) at 0.88 compared to VAE's 0.93. In terms of content similarity (CS), both models perform similarly, with DAE at 0.92 and VAE at 0.90. For the Amazon dataset, DAE and VAE continue to perform closely, with VAE slightly outperforming DAE in STA (0.82 vs. 0.72) and both showing strong performance in CS (0.92 for DAE and 0.90 for VAE)[5][8].

![Performance Comparison](image3)

In conclusion, while DAE tends to have a slight edge in style space separation, VAE demonstrates competitive performance in content space separation. Both models are effective in style transfer accuracy and content similarity across different datasets and latent spaces. These findings underscore the complementary strengths of the two models in different aspects of the task.

On the test dataset, the BERT model without any specific cues (BERT) shows a mean performance of 0.671 with a median of 0.712 and a maximum of 0.770. When the 'not' cue is considered (BERT (W)), the mean performance slightly drops to 0.656, with a median of 0.675 and a maximum of 0.712. ![Table of Adversarial Performance](image3)

The overall productivity and coverage metrics across different datasets (Train, Validation, and Test) indicate that while the cue 'not' offers some utility in traditional test settings (as shown by the test dataset results), it fails to provide the same advantage in adversarial settings, where the negation and swapping of labels make the models less effective in leveraging such cues.

This comparative analysis highlights the importance of robust evaluation methods that go beyond traditional test settings to ensure comprehensive model performance assessment.

[QUESTION] How do different control techniques impact the engagingness and conversational aspects of generated responses in dialogue models?
<<<EVIDENCE>>>

Different control techniques in dialogue models influence the engagingness and various conversational aspects of the generated responses. Here’s a detailed analysis based on the provided evidence from the document pages and figures. 

### Engagingness and Control Techniques

The engagingness of dialogue responses is influenced by various control techniques like weighted decoding (WD), specificity control (WD), and question-asking control (CT). Figure 3 illustrates the differences in engagingness across these techniques: 

![Engagingness](image3)

- **Greedy Search** and **Beam Search** models show lower engagingness compared to human interactions.
- **Repetition-Controlled (WD)**, **Specificity-Controlled (WD)**, and **Question-Controlled (CT)** models achieve higher engagingness scores, with human interactions rated the highest. 

### Specificity and Question-Asking Controls

Specificity control and question-asking control levels impact engagingness significantly. The middle and right plots in Figure 3 show that: 

- **Specificity Control (WD)**: Adjusting specificity control levels can optimize engagingness. The highest engagingness is observed around a specificity control level of 4 to 6[1]. 
- **Question-Asking Control (CT)**: Managing the number of questions asked also influences engagingness. The optimal level is around 6 to 7 questions, aligning closely with human-level engagingness[12]. 

### Conversational Aspects

Figure 4 provides detailed insights into various conversational aspects evaluated by human judgments, such as avoiding repetition, interestingness, making sense, fluency, listening, inquisitiveness, and humanness: 

![Conversational Aspects](image8)

- **Avoiding Repetition**: Human and controlled models like **Repetition-Controlled (WD)** perform better in avoiding repetition compared to greedy and beam search models. 
- **Interestingness**: Specificity-controlled models appear more interesting, followed by question-controlled models. 
- **Making Sense**: Human interactions score highest, followed by repetition-controlled models. 
- **Fluency**: Fluency is best in human interactions, with repetition and specificity-controlled models also scoring high. 
- **Listening**: Human and specificity-controlled models are better at demonstrating listening skills. 
- **Inquisitiveness**: Question-controlled models show higher inquisitiveness scores, close to human interactions. 
- **Humanness**: Human interactions are rated highest in humanness, with controlled models lagging behind but still performing better than greedy and beam search models. 

### Detailed Examples

To further illustrate the impact of control techniques, here are examples from the weighted decoding responses: 

- **Figure 1** shows responses based on different weights for the input, “Yes, I’m studying law at the moment.” As the weight (Wt) increases from -5.0 to 10.0, the responses vary significantly, impacting their engagingness and informativeness (NIDF). 

![Weighted Decoding Responses](image5)

- **Figure 2** presents responses to the input question, “Do you go get coffee often?” with different weights and similarities (Sim). The responses show how varying weights can change the context and relevance of the answers. 

![Weighted Decoding Coffee Responses](image6)

In conclusion, different control techniques significantly impact the engagingness and various conversational aspects of dialogue responses. Understanding these impacts helps in optimizing dialogue models for better human-like interactions.

[QUESTION] What is effective tax ratio of Best Buy for for the fiscal year ending January 28, 2023?Answer in percentage term, round to one decimal places.
<<<EVIDENCE>>>

The effective tax ratio is calculated by dividing the income tax expense by the earnings before income tax expense and equity in income of affiliates. For the fiscal year ending January 28, 2023, the relevant figures are:

- **Income tax expense**: $370 million
- **Earnings before income tax expense and equity in income of affiliates**: $1,788 million

The effective tax ratio is calculated as follows:

\[
\text{Effective Tax Ratio} = \left( \frac{\text{Income Tax Expense}}{\text{Earnings Before Income Tax Expense and Equity in Income of Affiliates}} \right) \times 100
\]

\[
\text{Effective Tax Ratio} = \left( \frac{370}{1,788} \right) \times 100 \approx 20.7\%
\]

Therefore, the effective tax ratio for Best Buy for the fiscal year ending January 28, 2023, is approximately **20.7%**.

### Climate Change
The potential impacts of climate change include supply constraints, increased costs, and damage to reputation. To address these issues, Nestlé has implemented the following measures:

- **Regenerative Agricultural Practices**: Nestlé promotes regenerative agricultural practices to support local rural development and ensure a sustainable supply chain.
- **Climate Adaptation and Mitigation Actions**: Nestlé has outlined actions in its 'Nestlé Net Zero Roadmap' to adapt to and mitigate the effects of climate change, such as adopting the TCFD (Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures) framework.

### Consumer Preferences
The potential impacts of failing to anticipate consumer preferences include negative effects on reputation, loss of market share, and failure to achieve growth targets. Nestlé has taken the following steps to mitigate these risks:

- **Consumer-Centric Innovations**: By strengthening the consumer-centricity of its innovation process, Nestlé aims to better align its products with evolving consumer preferences.
- **Improving Affordability of Safe and Healthy Food**: Nestlé focuses on applying scientific and nutritional know-how to enhance the accessibility and affordability of safe and nutritious food options.

### Net Income

- **2018:** Tesla reported a net loss of $1,063 million.
- **2019:** The net loss reduced to $775 million.
- **2020:** Tesla achieved a net income of $862 million.

The improvement in net income over the period can be associated with an increase in revenues, particularly from automotive sales[7] and energy generation, as well as better management of operating expenses.

### Comprehensive Income

- **2018:** Comprehensive income was a loss of $1,105 million.
- **2019:** It improved slightly to a loss of $803 million.

The move to a positive comprehensive income in 2020 was significantly influenced by a positive foreign currency translation adjustment of $399 million, which was a reversal from the losses in 2018 and 2019[1].

### Contributing Factors

1. **Foreign Currency Translation Adjustment:** This had a positive impact of $399 million in 2020, compared to losses in prior years[1].
2. **Net Income Improvement:** Driven by higher sales, especially in the automotive sector[7], and operational efficiencies.
3. **Attribution to Common Stockholders:** The comprehensive income attributable to common stockholders improved to $1,120 million in 2020 from a loss in previous years[10].

Overall, Tesla's financial turnaround from losses to profitability from 2018 to 2020 was largely due to increased revenue, controlled costs, and favorable currency adjustments.

**Weighted Decoding: Specificity Control**
Weighted decoding modifies the response by applying different weights, which influence the uniqueness and relevance of the response. For instance, in Figure 1, varying weights produce responses with different Normalized Inverse Document Frequency (NIDF) scores, reflecting the specificity of responses. Higher weights tend to generate more unique and specific responses, such as the response with a weight of 10.0, which produces a highly unique but nonsensical output[3][11].

![Figure 1](image6)

**Conditional Training: Question-Asking Control**
Conditional training, on the other hand, controls the probability of generating questions by adjusting a control variable. This method ensures that the model can produce outputs with a desired attribute, such as the presence of questions, without introducing unintended artifacts. Figure 3 demonstrates how conditional training effectively modulates the percentage of utterances containing a question mark ('?')[5]. The

passages.text: [5] For conditional training, we regard an utterance  $y$   as containing a question if and only if    $y$   con- tains a question mark. We train our CT model on a control variable    $z$   with 11 possible values:  $\{0,\hdots,10\}$  . As discussed in Section  5 , we wish to control question-asking at the distributional, di- alogue level, rather than at the binary, utterance level. Thus the setting    $z=i$   means that the model should produce, on average, utterances contain- ing ‘?’ with probability    $i/10$  . During training we randomly assign examples to buckets such that each bucket  $i$   is trained on examples with the cor- rect proportion of questions   $(i/10)$  , and all buckets have the same amount of training examples.

[12] In conversation, it’s generally desirable to produce a response that is related to the partner’s last utter- ance; for example if the partner says  My grandfa- ther died last month , it is appropriate to say  I’m so sorry. Were you close to your grandfather?  How- ever, our baseline model frequently responds with unrelated utterances like  Do you have any pets?

[QUESTION] How did the financial and production performance of copper and iron ore compare between FY2020 and FY2021?
<<<EVIDENCE>>>

The financial and production performance of copper and iron ore between FY2020 and FY2021 show distinct trends for each commodity. Here's a detailed comparison based on the provided data and figures: 

### Copper Performance

In FY2021, the revenue from copper increased to $15,726 million from $10,666 million in FY2020. The Underlying EBITDA also saw a significant rise from $4,347 million in FY2020 to $8,489 million in FY2021. However, the total copper production experienced a decline, dropping from 1,724 kilotonnes in FY2020 to 1,636 kilotonnes in FY2021. The average realised price for copper also increased from $2.50/lb in FY2020 to $3.81/lb in FY2021.

![Copper Performance](image4)

### Iron Ore Performance

For iron ore, the revenue soared to $34,475 million in FY2021, up from $20,797 million in FY2020. The Underlying EBITDA rose significantly from $14,554 million in FY2020 to $26,278 million in FY2021. The total iron ore production also increased from 248 million tonnes in FY2020 to 254 million tonnes in FY2021. The average realised price for iron ore witnessed a substantial rise from $77.36/wmt in FY2020 to $130.56/wmt in FY2021.

![Iron Ore Performance](image6)

### Escondida Unit Costs

The revenue from Escondida in FY2021 was $9,470 million, up from $6,719 million in FY2020. The Underlying EBITDA also increased from $3,535 million in FY2020 to $6,483 million in FY2021. Despite these revenue increases, gross costs decreased slightly from $3,184 million in FY2020 to $2,987 million in FY2021, leading to a decrease in net costs from $2,599 million in FY2020 to $2,347 million in FY2021. The cost per pound of copper also slightly decreased from $1.01 in FY2020 to $1.00 in FY2021.[8]

![Escondida Unit Costs](image2)

### WAIO Unit Costs

The revenue for WAIO also increased significantly, from $20,663 million in FY2020 to $34,337 million in FY2021. The Underlying EBITDA rose from $14,508 million in FY2020 to $26,270 million in FY2021. Gross costs increased from $6,155 million in FY2020 to $8,067 million in FY2021, and net costs rose from $3,165 million in FY2020 to $3,735 million in FY2021. The cost per tonne also increased from $12.63 in FY2020 to $14.82 in FY2021.

![WAIO Unit Costs](image7)

### Summary

- **Copper**: Increase in revenue and EBITDA, but a decrease in production. Average realised prices for copper increased.
- **Iron Ore**: Significant increases in revenue, EBITDA, production, and average realised prices.
- **Escondida**: Increase in revenue and EBITDA with a slight decrease in gross costs and net costs.
- **WAIO**: Significant increase in revenue and EBITDA, with increases in both gross and net costs as well as the cost per tonne.

These comparisons illustrate that while both commodities experienced revenue and EBITDA growth, iron ore demonstrated a more robust increase in production and realised prices compared to copper.

These results highlight the varying degrees of alignment between automatic metrics and human evaluations, with formality and fluency being the most reliable metrics according to human judgment[5][8], while BLEU and PINC show weaker relationships[1]. This analysis can guide the selection and improvement of automatic metrics based on their correlation with human assessments.

passages.text: [9] Evaluating Style Transfer: The problem of style transfer falls under the category of natu- ral language generation tasks such as machine translation, paraphrasing, etc. Previous work on style transfer ( Xu et al. ,  2012 ;  Jhamtani et al. , 2017 ;  Niu et al. ,  2017 ;  Sennrich et al. ,  2016a ) has re-purposed the MT metric BLEU ( Papineni et al. , 2002 ) and the paraphrase metric PINC ( Chen and Dolan ,  2011 ) for evaluation. Additionally, X U 12 introduce three new automatic style metrics based on cosine similarity, language model and logistic regression that measure the degree to which the output matches the target style. Under human based evaluation, on the other hand, there has been work on a more ﬁne grained evaluation where human judgments were separately collected for adequacy, ﬂuency and style ( Xu et al. ,  2012 ; Niu et al. ,  2017 ). In our work, we conduct a more thorough evaluation where we evaluate model outputs on the three criteria of  formality ,  ﬂuency and  meaning  using both automatic metrics and human judgments.

[6] Quantitative Analysis: While rewriting sen- tences more formally, humans tend to make a wide range of lexical/character-level edits. In Figure  1 , we plot the distribution of the character-level Lev- enshtein edit distance between the original infor- mal and the formal rewrites in the train set and observe a standard deviation of    $\sigma=19.39$   with a mean  $\mu=28.85$  . Next, we look at the difference in the formality level of the original informal and the formal rewrites in GYAFC. We ﬁnd that the classiﬁer trained on the  Answers  genre of PT16 dataset correlates poorly (Spearman  $\rho\,{=}\,0.38)$  ) with human judgments when tested on our domain spe- ciﬁc datasets. Hence, we collect formality judg- ments on a scale of  $^{-3}$   to  $+1$  , similar to PT16, for an additional 5000 sentences each from both do- mains and obtain a formality classiﬁer with higher correlation (Spearman    $\rho=0.56)$  ). We use this re- trained classiﬁer for our evaluation in    $\S5$   as well.

[5] We report the spearman rank correlation co- efﬁcient between automatic metrics and human judgments in Table  6 . For  formality ,  ﬂuency  and meaning , the correlation is with their respective human judgments whereas for BLEU, TERp and PINC, the correlation is with the overall ranking.

[1] We see that the formality and the ﬂuency met- rics correlate moderately well while the mean- ing metric correlates comparatively poorly. To be fair, the H E 15 classiﬁer was trained on the STS dataset which contains more formal writ- ing than informal. BLEU correlates moderately well (better than what X U 12 observed for the Shakespeare task) whereas the correlation drops for TERp. PINC, on the other hand, correlates very poorly with a positive correlation with rank when it should have a negative correlation with rank, just like BLEU. This sheds light on the fact that PINC, on its own, is not a good metric for style transfer since it prefers lexical edits at the cost of meaning changes. In the Shakespeare task, X U 12 did observe a higher correlation with PINC (0.41) although the correlation was not with over- all system ranking but rather only on the style met- ric. Moreover, in the Shakespeare task, changing the text is more favorable than in formality.
